lesson_title: A Hosepipe, a Lawn and the Planet's Heat Engine
hook_text: The sun hits the South Pole as hard as it hits Giyani. So why does only one of them freeze?
clip_script: Point a hosepipe straight down at the lawn and you soak one small circle of grass until it floods. Now swing the nozzle so the water flies out at a low angle: the same flow spreads into a long, thin, barely damp stripe. Not a drop was lost — it was simply shared across more lawn. That is the equator and the poles in one picture. The sun delivers the same beam everywhere, but near the equator it arrives almost straight down and drenches a small patch, while at the poles the earth's curve lays the ground back so the same beam smears into a weak stripe. And the poles get cheated a second time, because slanted light travels the long way through the atmosphere — like walking the full length of a packed school corridor instead of cutting straight across — losing a share to the crowd at every step. Then colour finishes it: snow and ice are the palest surfaces on the planet and fling back up to nine-tenths of their sunlight, while the dark ocean keeps almost everything, the way a black tracksuit cooks on sports day while white shirts stay cool. Soaked circle, damp stripe, white bounce, dark soak. That is why the tropics run a surplus, the poles run a deficit — and why every wind and every current on earth is part of the delivery system carrying the difference.
visual_style: A hosepipe soaking a tight circle then sweeping into a long faint stripe, morphing into sun rays on a curved globe; a corridor crowd thinning a beam of light; split shot of a white shirt and a black tracksuit shimmering on a school field.
mood: Curious and hands-on, opening out to planetary scale.
pacing: Slow reveal on the hosepipe swing, quick beats for path length and albedo, wide confident close.
